useful_analysis: Candidate final policy should minimize critical-path writes near hard cap.
Pre-arm at start makes scheduler continuity independent of late-turn scheduler availability.
A soft cutoff should eventually be based on observed unit-duration distribution rather than a fixed intuition.
Close reserve should use an upper-tail statistic once enough samples exist; median alone under-protects noisy closes.
Rollback should trigger on increased duration-failure rate or unresolved failure at/below cap.
Universal cap claims require representative workload profiles near the candidate boundary.
An I/O-heavy profile may expose lower practical limits than reasoning-heavy work because checkpoint latency sits on the close path.
Conversely, a reasoning-heavy unit can create admission overshoot if it is not interruptible at a safe boundary.
P2 may be the best complexity baseline because it bounds late-unit size without requiring accurate per-unit prediction.
P3 becomes attractive only if unit-duration estimates are calibrated enough to recover capacity without increasing close failures.
P4 should be rejected if its adaptation overhead or instability offsets small utilization gains.
These policy hypotheses are provisional and do not affect the current Phase-A boundary classification.
